books.title: Codex Tenebrarum
books.author: Brother Aldric of the Black Cloister
books.publisher: Copied by candlelight at St. Vitus-in-the-Dark, Bohemia
books.publication_history: Only three copies are known. The first was burned in 1214 by order of the Bishop of Prague. A second surfaced in a Venetian antiquarian's estate in 1789 and vanished shortly after cataloging. The surviving copy is chained to a lectern in a private Alpine collection.
books.synopsis: A monastic catalog of shadows that have detached themselves from their owners and begun to live independent lives in the corners of cathedrals.
books.review_excerpt: The shadows in my chamber moved differently after I closed it. — Anonymous bibliographer
books.detailed_history_1: Codex Tenebrarum, attributed to Brother Aldric of the Black Cloister and conventionally dated to approximately 1187, is described in the few surviving references as a monastic catalogus umbrarum, a systematic account of shadows that had separated from their human owners and acquired independent existence within churches, crypts, and abandoned religious houses. Aldric was reputedly a Benedictine copyist attached to an obscure foundation somewhere in the borderlands between the Empire and the eastern kingdoms, though later cataloguers disagree on whether the “Black Cloister” was a monastery, a scriptorium, or merely Aldric's name for the subterranean portion of a larger abbey. In his surviving colophon, quoted only once by the fourteenth-century antiquarian Petrus Maleficus, Aldric claimed that the shadows first revealed themselves to him during a winter vigil, when he observed that the silhouettes cast by twelve sleeping monks continued to move after the brothers had become still. What followed was, according to tradition, seven years of observation and clandestine inquiry.
books.detailed_history_2: The manuscript classified these entities by temperament, habitat, and degree of separation, from harmless “echo-shadows” that merely repeated forgotten gestures to the dreadful umbrae sine corpore, which possessed no known owner and gathered in the corners of cathedral vaults “where no lamp, moon, or sun had ever consented to shine.” The original codex was reportedly written on unusually thin, darkened vellum and bound between oak boards covered in cracked black leather. Its illuminations employed silver, soot, verdigris, and an ink said to contain powdered bone; several depicted architectural interiors in which the painted shadows extend beyond the objects that should have cast them. Cataloguers repeatedly mention stains resembling fingerprints but appearing in places too narrow for a human hand, as well as extensive water damage that somehow spared the text while erasing portions of the margins.
books.detailed_history_3: The final gatherings were said to have been deliberately cut away, leaving a ragged wound in the binding and a persistent uncertainty regarding what Aldric eventually discovered. Its condemnation began, according to ecclesiastical records of doubtful completeness, when copies circulated among cathedral scholars in the early thirteenth century. The book's central proposition, that a human shadow might survive its owner and retain memories, desires, or even theological opinions, was considered both heretical and dangerously close to asserting an independent soul within created darkness.
books.detailed_history_4: Several ecclesiastical authorities attempted to suppress it, while later inquisitorial inventories listed it among works non solum legendi prohibiti, sed etiam videndi vitandi, texts forbidden not merely to be read but, curiously, to be seen. Destruction proved unreliable. One copy reportedly survived immersion in a monastery cistern; another was burned in Avignon, after which the ashes were found arranged overnight in the outline of an open book.
books.detailed_history_5: The scholar Matthaeus Venn, who attempted the first Latin-to-French translation in 1489, vanished from his locked study, leaving only his unfinished manuscript and a second, unfamiliar shadow cast upon the wall. In 1731, the antiquarian Sir Alistair Wren attempted a scholarly edition, but destroyed his notes after reporting that his own silhouette had begun to appear several seconds late. The manuscript itself passed through the hands of collectors, renegade clerics, and at least one architect whose cathedral renovations were blamed for the disappearance of seventeen laborers beneath a newly opened transept.
books.detailed_history_6: Its present whereabouts remain unknown. The most persistent rumor places it in an uncatalogued collection beneath a former monastery, sealed inside a reliquary chest because no shelf could contain it without eventually acquiring an additional shadow. A more troubling tradition maintains that the Codex Tenebrarum no longer exists as a single volume at all: its pages have separated, dispersed through libraries and private collections, and now wait in darkness for the book to reassemble itself.

books.title: Das Buch der letzten Atemzüge
books.author: Hildebrandt der Stille
books.publisher: Scriptorium of the forsaken abbey at Thule
books.publication_history: Discovered in 1843 inside a sealed Bavarian tomb. The translator went mute three weeks after completing his work and never wrote again. Two subsequent editions were suppressed by imperial decree.
books.synopsis: A collection of final breaths captured in small glass vials, each accompanied by instructions for speaking with the person who exhaled it.
books.review_excerpt: To read it aloud is to invite the dead to finish the sentence. — Dr. Emil Voss
books.detailed_history_1: Das Buch der letzten Atemzüge, attributed to the otherwise obscure German mystic Hildebrandt der Stille and tentatively dated to the final decades of the thirteenth century, is among the strangest funerary manuscripts preserved in the occult bibliographies of Central Europe. Hildebrandt is believed to have been a lay brother or itinerant physician attached at various times to monasteries along the upper Rhine, though no ecclesiastical register securely identifies him. The manuscript's title is generally rendered as The Book of the Last Breaths, and its original purpose appears to have been neither devotional nor medical. Hildebrandt claimed to have discovered that the final exhalation of a dying person did not immediately disperse, but remained for a brief interval as a “memory of the body,” capable of being captured within a sealed glass vessel.
books.detailed_history_2: Each breath was supposedly accompanied by a precise ritual describing how the deceased might subsequently be addressed: the vessel was to be warmed between the hands, opened only in darkness, and spoken to using the dead person's baptismal name. According to the text, the resulting voice was not always audible in the ordinary sense. Some witnesses described answers heard inside the skull, while others reported that the glass itself began to whisper. Hildebrandt warned repeatedly that the dead “do not become more truthful merely because they have died,” and that certain final breaths belonged to persons who had already begun speaking to something else before death.
books.detailed_history_3: The surviving volume is a narrow quarto bound in pale, smoke-stained vellum over warped beech boards, its pages unusually translucent and carrying a persistent odor variously described as lavender, wet stone, and extinguished candles. The original manuscript is said to have contained seventy-two small glass vials, each secured within a recessed compartment in the binding or accompanying wooden case. Only nineteen are known to have survived into modern inventories, and several are reported to contain a dark condensation that does not evaporate even when the vessels are opened. The illuminations are remarkably restrained: portraits of the deceased appear in the margins, but their mouths have been painted shut with black pigment, while tiny silver lines emerge from their nostrils and disappear into the illustrations of the corresponding vials.
books.detailed_history_4: The book became particularly notorious after Hildebrandt's account was condemned as necromancy by several ecclesiastical authorities. The University of Paris reportedly prohibited its circulation, while local bishops ordered known copies surrendered and burned. Suppression was complicated by the fact that readers were reluctant to destroy the vessels themselves. One sixteenth-century collector, Konrad Eber, allegedly opened a vial belonging to an unnamed child and heard a voice asking why the room had become so much larger.
books.detailed_history_5: Eber's household subsequently reported footsteps in empty rooms and the sound of breathing beneath locked doors. In 1642, a Jesuit scholar attempted to translate the work into Latin and died before completing the chapter concerning “breaths that remember more than one death.” His unfinished translation was found beside him, every page covered by the same sentence in three different hands. During the nineteenth century, several occultists searched for the surviving vials, believing they could be used to question historical figures. Their efforts ended abruptly after a private séance in Prague produced seventeen voices from a single bottle.
books.detailed_history_6: The current whereabouts of Das Buch der letzten Atemzüge are disputed. The most credible twentieth-century reference places the manuscript in a sealed collection somewhere in Bavaria, with the surviving vials stored separately under conditions of permanent darkness. A persistent rumor among collectors, however, claims that one vial remains empty by design. Its label bears no name, only a date that has never occurred.

books.title: Liber Mundi Invisibilis
books.author: Al-Kindi's unknown pupil
books.publisher: House of Wisdom, Baghdad; later smuggled west
books.publication_history: Translated into Latin in 1232 by an apostate Franciscan. The Latin version was declared anathema at the Council of Lyons. The Arabic original was reportedly destroyed during the Mongol sack of Baghdad.
books.synopsis: A mathematical proof that the visible world is a thin scum atop an older, hungrier geometry that occasionally bleeds through at certain angles.
books.review_excerpt: Euclid would have wept blood. — Vatican Index entry
books.detailed_history_1: Liber Mundi Invisibilis, conventionally dated to the late ninth or early tenth century, is attributed in later Arabic bibliographies to an otherwise unnamed pupil of Al-Kindi, the celebrated philosopher of Baghdad. No contemporary source identifies the author, and the phrase Al-Kindi's unknown pupil appears to have been added by a much later cataloguer, perhaps to lend authority to a work that had already acquired an ominous reputation.
books.detailed_history_2: The manuscript presents itself as a treatise in geometry, optics, and mathematical philosophy, beginning with familiar propositions concerning planes, angles, and the perception of light before gradually introducing a second geometry concealed beneath ordinary space. According to its central argument, the visible world is not the true geometric structure of creation but a superficial layer, described in one surviving Arabic gloss as “the skin upon the world.”
books.detailed_history_3: Beneath it lies an older arrangement of planes, angles, and dimensions governed by mathematical relationships that human perception normally cannot apprehend. Certain intersections, viewed from precisely prescribed angles, supposedly allow this underlying geometry to become visible. The author insists that these appearances are not illusions but brief failures of the world's concealment. More disturbing are his final propositions, which suggest that the hidden geometry is not merely ancient but alive, and that the distortions observed at certain angles represent pressure from something attempting to enter ordinary space.
books.detailed_history_4: The surviving manuscript is a small, exceptionally heavy codex written in black and reddish-brown ink on yellowed parchment, with diagrams occupying far more space than the accompanying text. Its geometric figures are peculiar even by medieval standards: circles that do not close, triangles whose fourth sides appear only in marginal notes, and perspective drawings that depict architectural structures impossible to construct in three dimensions. Several diagrams contain tiny annotations instructing the reader to tilt the page toward a lamp or view it from beneath the edge of a table. Reports concerning the manuscript become increasingly disturbing after the twelfth century.
books.detailed_history_5: A Persian astronomer attempting to verify its propositions reportedly discovered that the shadow cast by a straightedge had developed a second angle not present in the object itself. A copyist in Damascus was said to have gone blind after completing the “Ninth Figure,” although witnesses claimed that he continued describing invisible shapes in the air until his death. The work was condemned by religious scholars for combining illicit speculation with a cosmology that placed mathematical necessity above divine creation, while several copies were reportedly seized and destroyed by court-appointed officials. One surviving Latin translation, produced in the seventeenth century, was suppressed after its translator annotated the margins with increasingly frantic calculations and eventually wrote that the diagrams “change when nobody is looking.”
books.detailed_history_6: Modern collectors consider the original Liber Mundi Invisibilis lost, although fragments have periodically surfaced in private collections from Cairo to Prague. The most persistent account places the manuscript in a locked astronomical archive somewhere in Istanbul, where it is supposedly kept wrapped in black cloth and never displayed flat. According to an unverified nineteenth-century inventory, the final page contains no writing at all, only a single geometric figure that appears to occupy different positions on the parchment depending upon the angle from which it is viewed. The inventory adds one final notation in Latin: Do not seek the angle from which it is complete.

books.title: Malleus Deorum Silentium
books.author: Sister Praetextata of Aquileia
books.publisher: Illicit press beneath the catacombs of Rome
books.publication_history: Written by a nun who claimed to have heard the gods refuse to speak. Buried with her in a lead coffin; exhumed in 1567 and immediately re-interred without the book. A single illuminated page survives in the Vatican's sealed annex.
books.synopsis: An argument that the silence of the divine is not absence but a deliberate withholding, and that prayer is slowly widening the wound that silence covers.
books.review_excerpt: The only heresy that frightens theologians into agreement. — Cardinal Bembo
books.detailed_history_1: The Malleus Deorum Silentium is traditionally dated to 1044 and attributed to Sister Praetextata of Aquileia, a Benedictine scholar attached to a convent outside the ruined ecclesiastical quarter of Aquileia. Little is known of Praetextata beyond references to her in two monastic inventories, both of which describe her as “learned beyond the permitted measure.” According to the manuscript's surviving prologue, Praetextata spent nine years examining unanswered prayers, particularly those offered during plague, famine, and siege. Her conclusion was profoundly unorthodox: divine silence was not evidence of divine absence, but evidence of something deliberately concealed behind the fabric of creation.
books.detailed_history_2: The surviving codex is unusually small for a theological treatise, consisting of approximately 137 leaves of thin, grayish vellum bound between warped alder boards covered in blackened calfskin. The leather bears no title, clasp, or ornamentation. Instead, a shallow depression resembling a thumbprint appears on the front cover and reportedly never accumulates dust. The manuscript's illuminations are sparse and deliberately unfinished. Halos are painted around empty spaces rather than figures, while several depictions of saints show them kneeling before immense fields of unpainted parchment.
books.detailed_history_3: The theological danger of the Malleus Deorum Silentium was recognized soon after its circulation beyond Praetextata's convent. Its assertion that unanswered prayer actively altered the boundary between the divine and material worlds was condemned as both heretical and blasphemous. More troubling still was Praetextata's suggestion that what waited beyond that boundary might not be God, but an older presence whose silence had been mistaken for divine transcendence.
books.detailed_history_4: The codex disappeared from Aquileia during the upheavals of the twelfth century and resurfaced nearly two hundred years later in the library of a noble family near Verona. According to the family's chronicle, the book was kept locked in an iron chest after three members of the household independently reported hearing a congregation whispering inside the chapel after midnight, despite the chapel having been abandoned for decades.
books.detailed_history_5: At least four attempts have been made to destroy the Malleus Deorum Silentium. The earliest known copy was burned at a monastery near Padua, but the monks reportedly discovered that several passages had appeared on otherwise blank pages of unrelated books throughout the library. A sixteenth-century scholar attempted to produce a complete Latin edition from an Aquileian fragment and died after completing the chapter concerning the “First Prayer.” His assistants found him seated at his desk, hands folded, listening intently to an empty corner of the room.
books.detailed_history_6: The present whereabouts of the Malleus Deorum Silentium are unknown. The last authenticated sighting occurred in 1913, when a Viennese collector reportedly purchased the codex from an Italian priest who claimed that it had been kept for generations beneath a monastery altar. The collector's house burned six weeks later. Investigators found the library destroyed but the manuscript absent, despite its having been stored inside a steel safe.

books.title: Chronicon Subterraneum
books.author: Thorkell the Worm-Tongued
books.publisher: Carved and later inked at Reykjavik black chapel
books.publication_history: Icelandic church authorities attempted to burn every copy in 1220. A fragment was later found sewn into the sail of a drifting longship with no crew. The complete text was transcribed in 1902 from a rune-stick cache.
books.synopsis: A history of the civilizations that existed beneath Europe before the ice retreated, written by those who claimed to have descended and returned changed.
books.review_excerpt: The earth is older than our saints admit, and it remembers. — Icelandic Antiquarian Society
books.detailed_history_1: The Chronicon Subterraneum is attributed to Thorkell the Worm-Tongued, a Norse cleric and itinerant scribe believed to have lived sometime during the late eleventh century, although the earliest references to him are themselves uncertain. The manuscript claims to record the testimony of several men who descended through caverns beneath northern Europe and returned years later, despite having aged only weeks. According to Thorkell's introduction, these travelers described vast civilizations existing beneath the earth before the retreat of the ice, possessing cities of black stone, languages without spoken words, and calendars measured according to geological rather than celestial cycles. Thorkell insisted that their accounts were not myths but fragments of a history older than mankind's accepted chronology, and that the returned explorers had brought back knowledge that had “changed the shape of their souls.”
books.detailed_history_2: The surviving codex is a thick, squat volume of dark vellum bound in seal skin over heavy oak boards. Its pages have an unusual granular texture, and several contain embedded fragments of pale mineral that catch the light like mica. The illuminations depict subterranean cities, enormous stairways descending into darkness, and pale figures standing beneath immense vaulted caverns; in several illustrations, the figures' faces have been carefully scraped away. The margins contain numerous worms, roots, and eyeless subterranean animals rendered in meticulous detail. Most disturbing is the ink used for several later additions, which has faded to a reddish-brown resembling dried blood. The book also emits a persistent odor of damp earth, even after centuries in dry storage.
books.detailed_history_3: The Chronicon Subterraneum attracted ecclesiastical condemnation because its chronology placed sophisticated civilizations beneath Europe thousands of years before the Creation date accepted by medieval theologians. More dangerous were its descriptions of beings who supposedly existed before humanity and whose knowledge of the surface world preceded the first human prophets. Several passages imply that the earliest European religions were distorted memories of encounters with these subterranean powers. Church authorities in Scandinavia and northern Germany ordered copies confiscated, while at least one bishop declared the work “a history written from beneath the world.” The manuscript was subsequently associated with forbidden pagan traditions, necromancy, and the heresy of believing that Creation possessed an inhabited underside.
books.detailed_history_4: During the fourteenth century, the manuscript reportedly belonged to a Danish nobleman whose estate contained a sealed cavern entrance discovered beneath his chapel. After reading the Chronicon, the nobleman ordered an expedition into the cavern. Of the eleven men who entered, three returned, carrying no provisions and speaking a dialect none could identify. They claimed that the others had remained below voluntarily. Within a year, all three disappeared. A later owner, the German antiquarian Matthias Greven, reportedly kept the codex chained to his desk and became obsessed with measuring the floors of his house. After his death, investigators discovered that he had excavated a perfectly circular shaft beneath his study, extending more than thirty meters into the earth despite having no engineering equipment capable of accomplishing the work.
books.detailed_history_5: At least five copies of the Chronicon Subterraneum are mentioned in medieval inventories, though none can now be located. One copy was burned at a monastery near Lund, after which monks reportedly found unfamiliar footprints appearing in the ashes each morning. In the seventeenth century, a scholar attempted to translate the manuscript's descriptions of the subterranean language and discovered that several passages could be read only when viewed upside down. His notes state that the translated text consisted largely of directions rather than historical accounts. He abandoned the project after realizing that the directions described the location of the monastery where he was working. Three weeks later, workers repairing the crypt uncovered a staircase descending beneath the foundations, which was immediately sealed.
books.detailed_history_6: The whereabouts of the original Chronicon Subterraneum remain unknown. The last credible record places it in the private collection of a Swedish antiquarian who disappeared in 1896 after announcing that he had located “the northern entrance.” His estate was found intact, but the manuscript and several surveying instruments were missing. Modern occult bibliographies variously claim that the book lies beneath a monastery in Iceland, inside a sealed chamber beneath Trondheim, or within a private collection in Copenhagen. The most persistent legend maintains that Thorkell's manuscript was never intended to describe where the subterranean civilizations were, but where they still are. According to this account, the final pages were deliberately written in reverse because Thorkell had discovered that the civilizations beneath Europe were not waiting for humanity to find them. They were waiting for the ice to return.

books.title: Vermis Mysteriorum
books.author: Caius Sempronius the Pale
books.publisher: Imperial scriptorium, later hidden beneath Pompeii
books.publication_history: Pulled from the ashes of Pompeii in 1785. The first owner died of worms in his sleep. The second donated it to a monastery, which buried it in a salt cellar. Current whereabouts unknown.
books.synopsis: A catalog of worms that do not eat earth but consume memory, identity, and eventually the names of the dead.
books.review_excerpt: I no longer remember why I began reading it. — Marginal note, 1791

books.title: Septem Sigilla Profundi
books.author: The Seven Anonymous Anchorites
books.publication_history: Each of the seven sections was copied by a different monk who never met the others. When assembled, the book is said to be exactly the length of a human spine. All known assemblies have ended in fire.
books.synopsis: Instructions for opening seven seals that should not exist, each seal corresponding to a sound the earth makes in its sleep.
books.review_excerpt: The binding creaks in seven distinct voices. — Inquisitor's report, 1312

books.title: Das Grauen aus den Kellern
books.author: Konrad von Nürnberg
books.publication_history: Printed in a run of forty copies on paper dyed with soot from plague fires. The city council seized the press and drowned it in the Pegnitz. A handful of copies survived in the walls of demolished houses.
books.synopsis: An account of the things that climb up from the cellars of Nuremberg when the chimneys stop smoking, and the bargains they offer homeowners.
books.review_excerpt: After reading it, no cellar door feels fully shut. — Herr Doktor Fleiss

books.title: Liber Ossium Sonantium
books.author: Ostanes the Chaldean, attributed
books.publisher: Copied from a Babylonian original in Alexandria
books.publication_history: Survived the burning of the Library of Alexandria because it was reportedly checked out by a merchant ship. Later found in a Coptic monastery, from which it disappeared in 882.
books.synopsis: A manual for arranging bones so they produce accurate prophecies, and for silencing them again before they begin to ask questions.
books.review_excerpt: The bones answered. I wish I had not asked. — Last entry of Brother Methodius

books.title: Fragmenta Antiquissima
books.author: Unknown; possibly pre-Phoenician
books.publisher: Recovered from a tin mine in Cornwall
books.publication_history: Unearthed by miners who reported the vein of tin sang while the book was removed. The Latin translation was added by a medieval monk whose hands reportedly never stopped trembling.
books.synopsis: Fragments of a far older text describing the stars before they were named and the prayers offered to the spaces between them.
books.review_excerpt: The original script resembles writing, but also teeth-marks. — Cornwall Mining Gazette

books.title: Grimoire des Verborgenen Königs
books.author: Eberhard der Schattenleser
books.publication_history: Commissioned by a claimant to the Bohemian throne who vanished the night the book was completed. The grimoire passed through seven royal houses; each owner died without heir.
books.synopsis: A handbook of rituals used by a king who ruled from behind his own throne, allowing his shadow to sign laws and command armies.
books.review_excerpt: Every copy attempts to bind itself to the nearest crown. — Imperial Censor's note

books.title: Tractatus de Portis Insomnium
books.author: Master Roger of Hereford
books.publication_history: Condemned at the Council of Oxford in 1240. The only complete copy was hidden inside the hollowed leg of a refectory table and discovered during Victorian restoration.
books.synopsis: A study of doors that appear only in dreams and the correct etiquette for knocking on them without being invited inside.
books.review_excerpt: I knocked once. The door is still open behind my eyelids. — Archdeacon Thwaite

books.title: Codex Lunae Mortuae
books.author: Arnaud de Montfaucon
books.publication_history: Printed on paper made from mulberry trees grown in lunar soil, according to the colophon. The first readers reported the pages glowed faintly during eclipses. Seized by the Inquisition in 1487.
books.synopsis: Star charts for a moon that died long ago, including predictions for when its corpse will finally complete its slow fall toward the earth.
books.review_excerpt: The tides respond to its pages, not to the living moon. — Astronomer's log

books.title: Liber Facierum Absconditarum
books.author: Ibn al-Haytham's apostate student
books.publication_history: Smuggled to Sicily in 1098. Emperor Frederick II ordered it locked in a tower without windows. A German translation surfaced during the Thirty Years' War and disappeared at the siege of Magdeburg.
books.synopsis: Instructions for seeing the faces that belong to empty spaces, and for remembering that some angles of reflection are not meant for human eyes.
books.review_excerpt: My mirror no longer shows only myself. — Count von Hohenlohe

books.title: Die Stimmen unter dem Boden
books.author: Anna von der Tiefe
books.publication_history: The printer's shop burned the morning after the final sheet was pulled. Anna was committed to an almshouse, where she whispered to the floor until her death. The book was banned in every German-speaking state.
books.synopsis: A woman's record of the voices she heard rising through the floorboards of Strasbourg, and the alphabet they taught her.
books.review_excerpt: The floor in my study answered when I read her alphabet. — Prof. W. Kraus

books.title: Mysterium Arcae Noctis
books.author: Brother Theodosius the Sleepless
books.publication_history: Kept in a sealed chest at Mount Athos for eight centuries. A photograph of a single page was published in 1924; the photographer later gouged out his own eyes.
books.synopsis: A description of the Ark that preceded Noah's: not a boat, but a coffin built to keep something awake while the world drowned.
books.review_excerpt: Even the photograph should not have been looked at. — Byzantine Studies Quarterly

books.title: Vocabularium Tenebrarum
books.author: Ephraim the Lexicographer
books.publisher: Antioch, scriptorium of the damned dictionary
books.publication_history: Ephraim reportedly went blind while compiling the letter Qoph. The dictionary was suppressed by both Byzantine and Islamic authorities. A single copy reached the Bodleian in 1689 and was immediately restricted.
books.synopsis: A dictionary of words that should exist but do not, with pronunciation guides and warnings about the thoughts that accompany their use.
books.review_excerpt: I learned three words. The third opened a door in my mouth. — Bodleian reader's complaint

books.title: Chronica Eorum qui Descenderunt
books.author: Decius Mus, chronicler of the Templars
books.publisher: Acre, before the fall; smuggled to Cyprus
books.publication_history: Written during the siege of Acre. The author is listed as having died defending the walls, yet the chronicle contains entries dated decades later. The Vatican copy is missing its final folio.
books.synopsis: A record of knights who descended into cisterns and caves beneath the Holy Land and returned with new devotions and older allegiances.
books.review_excerpt: The last page was not torn out. It was never written in this world. — Templar historian

books.title: Liber Aquarum Oblitarum
books.author: Hypatia's unnamed copyist
books.publication_history: Said to have been copied from a scroll that survived the Library's destruction. Found in a Venetian well in 1503. Anyone who drank from the well afterward spoke in verse for three days.
books.synopsis: A guide to waters that have forgotten their sources, including the rites required to make them remember or to ensure they never do.
books.review_excerpt: The water in my glass bent toward the page. — Paduan natural philosopher

books.title: Das Auge das nie schließt
books.author: Friedrich von Aue
books.publication_history: Bound in blue leather with a circular brass clasp. The heretic press was drowned in the Danube by the Swabian League. Fishermen in the area still report seeing an open eye in the water on certain nights.
books.synopsis: A manual for growing, feeding, and eventually disposing of an eye that watches on behalf of something that has no face.
books.review_excerpt: I covered the clasp. It watched through the leather. — Knight of the League

books.title: Liber Sanguinis Subterranei
books.author: Maria de la Sangre Oculta
books.publisher: Toledo, printed in a single night
books.publication_history: Printed during a single new-moon night; the ink was later found to contain iron salts consistent with blood diluted with groundwater. The author was burned by the Spanish Inquisition; her copy survived in a brick oven.
books.synopsis: A treatise on underground rivers that behave like bloodstreams and the organisms that swim in them, some of which resemble human organs.
books.review_excerpt: The pages are warm, and slightly damp, and do not fully dry. — Inquisitor's inventory

books.title: Codex Finis Mundi
books.author: The Last Librarian of Alexandria, attributed
books.publication_history: Brought to Europe by a Portuguese explorer who died of fever before reaching Lisbon. The codex changed hands thirteen times; each owner died on the anniversary of acquisition.
books.synopsis: A calendar of the world's endings, most of which have already happened without anyone noticing, and the one ending that is still scheduled.
books.review_excerpt: We are living in the margin between two of its pages. — Coptologist's note

books.title: Das Buch ohne Anfang
books.author: Unknown; first words are the middle of a sentence
books.publication_history: Bound in wood from a gallows. Scholars have identified the same anonymous hand in marginalia across Europe, but no two copies begin with the same sentence. The book appears to be missing its first page in every known copy.
books.synopsis: A grimoire that starts mid-ritual, forcing the reader to infer what came before and to wonder whether they have already performed the opening.
books.review_excerpt: I found my own handwriting in the margins, dated before my birth. — Collector's note

books.title: Testamentum Vaccae Stellarum
books.author: Baal-Hanan the Stargazer
books.publication_history: Hidden in a cave near the Dead Sea and rediscovered in 1952. The Bedouin who found it refused payment and would not touch the binding. It is now held under restricted access in Jerusalem.
books.synopsis: The testament of a star-worshipping cult that believed certain cattle were star-maps written in flesh, and the heresy of reading them.
books.review_excerpt: The cattle lowed when the cave was opened. They were miles away. — Archaeological report

books.title: De Cultu Serpentium Sapientium
books.author: Bishop Serapion the Unclean
books.publication_history: Authored by a bishop who was later anathematized and walled into a cistern. His book was buried with him; thieves recovered it in 1711. Since then it has been stolen from every library that tried to keep it.
books.synopsis: A liturgical manual for a church that worshipped the wisdom of serpents and performed communion with venom instead of wine.
books.review_excerpt: It has never stayed on the same shelf for more than seven years. — Curator's ledger
